newsitem.title: UK: N.Ireland Loyalists accused of planting bomb.
newsitem.headline: N.Ireland Loyalists accused of planting bomb.

text.p: Pro-British Loyalists tried to blow up a Belfast office of the IRA's political wing, Sinn Fein on Sunday, in an apparent breach of their 1994 ceasefire.
The British Broadcasting Corporation quoted Loyalist sources as saying the attempt was a "measured" response to attacks by their Irish Republican Army (IRA) foes, who seek to end British rule.

A complete breakdown of the Loyalists' 1994 ceasefire would return Northern Ireland to the tit-for-tat violence which reigned until both Loyalists and the IRA called a halt to their wars to pursue an Anglo-Irish peace initiative.

Security forces said they made safe the 40 kg (88-lb) bomb, which was driven to the New Lodge offices of Sinn Fein in a hijacked taxi on the day that Irish republicans commemorate the 1916 Dublin rising against British rule.

Britain's Northern Ireland Secretary, Sir Patrick Mayhew, condemned Loyalists for the attack but made no comment about whether it would affect the participation of their political spokesmen at Belfast peace talks which resume on June 3.

Two small political groups allied to Loyalist guerrilla organisations have claimed seats at the Belfast negotiations. Sinn Fein is excluded because of the IRA's ending of its own 17-month truce in February 1996.

Mayhew said in a statement that the New Lodge attack together with the IRA shooting of a policeman and an attempted IRA bomb attack against British troops at the weekend were the work of groups with no commitment to democracy.
"The message is that the organisations concerned still rely upon death and destruction to secure what they want in this democracy," he said.

The weekend violence underscored the tension in Northern Ireland on the eve of a Belfast parade by Protestants which signals the start of the annual "marching season," which is seen by minority Catholics as a show of Protestant domination.
Loyalists have been blamed for several previous attacks but their umbrella group, the Combined Loyalist Military Command, has not issued a statement saying the truce is officially over.
Weekend violence highlighted what Royal Ulster Constabulary police chief Ronnie Flanagan called a very dangerous situation in Northern Ireland since the end of the IRA truce.
Gerry Adams, the Sinn Fein President, told a Belfast rally that a British general election on May 1 offered the Northern Ireland electorate "a new opportunity to reconstruct the peace process."

He was apparently reacting to a weekend statement by Mo Mowlam, spokeswoman for Northern Ireland of the opposition Labour party, which seems set to topple Prime Minister John Major's Conservative government in the election.
Mowlam said that if the IRA ended its war against British rule immediately, it could claim a seat at the Belfast talks when they resume on June 3.

She said the months of April and May could be used to verify that a new IRA ceasefire was genuine, but Adams gave no hint that such a move was imminent and made no allusion to media speculation about a possible pre-election IRA ceasefire.

Sinn Fein's ideological foes, Protestant Unionist parties which want the province to stay British, say they will walk out of the Belfast talks if Sinn Fein enters because they do not believe the IRA will declare a complete end to guerrilla war.

Sinn Fein is contesting several seats in the poll to underline its support, estimated at around 15 per cent of the electorate. Party policy is not to take up seats it wins in the London parliament because it would entail allegiance to Britain.
